examples.input: Save a changed file, then the process is killed or the disk fills up partway through the write

results.1: The file holds either the complete old text or the complete new text. At worst a stray temp file is left next to it.
results.2: The file can be left cut off or empty, and the old content is lost.

context.in_practice: Both routes leave unchanged files alone. Route 1 writes the new version beside the original, flushes it to disk, copies over the original's permissions and then swaps it in, so anyone reading the file sees the old version or the new one and never a partial one. A side effect is that the file becomes a new file on disk, so hard links to the old file and some ownership details may not carry over. Route 2 overwrites the original directly. Anything other than a write error has already been checked before writing starts, so nothing breaks in normal use. The risk is limited to a crash, a full disk or another operating-system failure during the write itself. Route 3 was not considered.
context.stakes: If the program is interrupted, or the disk fills up while it is saving a changed file, the user could end up with a truncated or empty file instead of either the old version or the new one.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 costs a temp file, a disk flush and a file swap on every save, and needs more code to maintain. Route 2 is simpler and keeps the file's identity on disk, but a failure during the write can leave a half-written file. Route 3 was not considered.

plan_why: The routes differ only in how bytes reach disk: an atomic temp-file, fsync and os.replace versus writing in place. Under normal runs both produce the same file contents and the same output. The only visible differences would appear if the process crashed or hit an OS error mid-write, or with read-only files, symlinked or hard-linked config files, or file modes and inode identity. This sandbox cannot set up any of those: files are plain, created fresh with default permissions, there is no way to inject failures, and `show` prints only contents. So no command sequence would tell the routes apart.
routes: Temp file in the same directory, fsync, copy permissions, os.replace; only changed files are touched
Write in place with newline='' only when the text changed, no temp files
